intro.title: Learn autonomous racing
intro.overview: RoboRacer is a hands-on course in the foundations of autonomy: perception, planning and control, practiced on a 1/10-scale race car. Start in the simulator with ROS 2, build up through mapping, optimal control and reinforcement learning, then race what you wrote. Built for graduate and senior undergraduate students.
teaches: Analytic skills to recognize and reason about situations with moral content in the design of autonomous systems
not: A replacement for the semester-long graduate courses in the topics we cover
intro.note: This course integrates the concepts above and is not a beginner course in any of them. The material is best suited to graduate level, or at the very least a senior undergraduate course.
intro.community: Join the discussion on Slack. The workspace is for educators, collaborators and organizers.

syllabus.lead: A semester-long course. Run it as it stands, or pick and choose lectures to fit a quarter or shorter.

components.title: Lectures
components.body: Taught clab-style (classroom plus lab): each session pairs a lecture with tutorial or lab time.

components.title: Labs
components.body: Done outside class time. This is where students apply what the lectures teach.

components.title: Races
components.body: Three races, each testing a different part of the class: Race 1 on basic methods, Race 2 on advanced control, and the final race.

components.title: Final project
components.body: Students propose a problem and solve it on the RoboRacer vehicle system, in teams of 3 to 4 with different skills.

lecture1.title: Introduction to Autonomous Driving: Perception, Planning, Control
lecture1.overview: An introduction to the RoboRacer autonomous vehicle community. We give a brief tour of the world of autonomous racing and step through each lecture on perception, planning and control. By the end you will have had your first taste of the exciting world of autonomous systems.

outline.title: Perception, Planning & Control

grading.title: Grading
grading.lead: An autograder builds your code and runs it in the simulator, and TAs grade the videos. Your score appears on your repository minutes after you submit.

submit.title: How a submission works
submit.lead: Submissions are managed with Classroom 50. Push your work as often as you like; only a tag counts.

steps.title: Push your work
steps.body: Commit and push as often as you need. A plain push does not count as a submission.

steps.title: Push the submission tag
steps.body: Pushing a tag named submission starts the autograder.

steps.title: Read your score
steps.body: The autograder builds your package, checks it, runs it in the simulator, and posts your score as a Release on your repository a few minutes later.

steps.title: Resubmit by moving the tag
steps.body: Move the tag to a newer commit and push it again. Your best scored submission is the one that counts.

submit.code:
git push
git tag submission
git push origin submission

# to resubmit
git tag -f submission
git push --force origin submission
submit.team_note: From Lab 4 on, labs are done in teams. One repository per team, any member can push the tag, and it counts for the whole team.
submit.names_note: The autograder finds your work by name, so use the package, node, topic and launch file names each lab specifies.

items.title: It builds
items.body: Compilation is worth 10 to 30 points depending on the lab.

items.title: Logic, without the simulator
items.body: Your node is fed scans or poses (a corridor, a dead end, a car off its path) and must steer the right way each time.

items.title: Runs in the simulator
items.body: Your code drives laps in the grading simulator without touching a wall. A run that ends early earns partial credit for the distance covered.

items.title: TA-graded videos
items.body: Videos are linked from SUBMISSION.md: unlisted on YouTube, or on Google Drive shared as Anyone with the link can view.

sim.title: Simulator evaluations
sim.lead: Every lab that drives is graded the same way: your node runs on a track in the grading simulator while the autograder times the laps. The fastest clean lap goes to the class leaderboard, and the board replays the best runs.
